turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, sorry we're late, the robot by the garage is dead with the load shedding. Naledi's been really poorly, a cough and a fever.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Shame. Pop her up on the bed for me. How old is she now?
[SEG0003] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Four. She turned four in March and she's just gone into Grade R. Is this something she picked up there, do you think?
[SEG0004] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ag, don't start with the crèche. It's been going since Saturday already, at my house. I told you it wasn't a little sniffle.
[SEG0005] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ma, no. The cough started Wednesday. That's three days. Wednesday night she was hot, that's when the fever showed up.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm not deaf, my girl. Saturday she was coughing in my lounge, you can ask anyone. That's five days, not three.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. So you two aren't meeting on the start date, cough somewhere in that window. Has she been drinking alright?
[SEG0008] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sips, yes, juice and water. She's not eating much at all. No vomiting, though, not once.
[SEG0009] person_4 (PATIENT): Mommy... sore.
[SEG0010] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ja, her throat's sore, she keeps telling me. She points at it and then she cries.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Naledi, sweetheart, is it your tummy that's sore, or your throat?
[SEG0012] person_4 (PATIENT): Throat. No.

[SEG0013] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And Doctor, the fever number. Her mother has been saying thirty nine point two since last night. I was looking at that thermometer with my own eyes. It was thirty eight, on the dot. She reads the lines wrong.
[SEG0014] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I do not read them wrong. It was thirty nine point two. She was burning up, I'm not making it up.

[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to pick a winner on a home thermometer you both saw differently. Mine, just now, ear: thirty eight point four. Pulse is one hundred and twenty four. Respiratory rate twenty six. Saturation ninety seven percent on air.
[SEG0016] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Is thirty eight point four bad? Does she need an antibiotic? Please, it's not pneumonia, is it? I can't do a hospital admission, not with work the way it is.

[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me think it through with you, not jump. Fever and cough at four is usually a viral upper airway infection. It can also be the beginning of a chest infection. I'm not prepared to call it pneumonia from the doorway, and I won't say it isn't bacterial until I've listened. Croup is unlikely without a bark. Let's see what the chest actually does, hey.
[SEG0018] person_4 (PATIENT): Don't want.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): I know, almost done. Mouth open... throat's a bit red. Both ears are clear. Chest is clear, no crackles, no wheeze, and she's not pulling in under the ribs.
[SEG0020] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So the chest is fine? Her father had asthma, I'm always waiting for that wheeze. Shame, man.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Asthma in the family makes me listen twice, but there's no wheeze today, so I'm not putting that label on her from one illness.

[SEG0022] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Last winter, at the clinic, they did a chest x-ray for that other bad cough. The sister said it was borderline. Not pneumonia, she said, just borderline. Does that change today?

[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): A film someone called borderline last winter doesn't tell me what this is. I'm not repeating the x-ray today. If she is not turning the corner, we can think about one later, not now.
[SEG0024] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Tell him what we gave, Ma, before we fight again. I gave Panado syrup by mouth, one medicine spoon, every six hours, since yesterday.
[SEG0025] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You filled that spoon twice. Two spoons. And I swear the bottle was the ibuprofen, the Nurofen one, not the Panado.
[SEG0026] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It was Panado, the pink syrup. I never opened the ibuprofen. One spoon, not two. I'm completely sure about the spoon.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ag, alright. The bottles look the same when the light's off, maybe I mixed the name up. It was the pink one. But it was two spoons, I watched you, not one.
[SEG0028] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So did I underdose her with one spoon? Is that too little? Can I add ibuprofen tonight if she's still hot? What if I give too much, what happens then?

[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): This is why kitchen spoons cause wars. Use the syringe that comes in the box: ten ml of the one hundred and twenty milligram per five ml Panado, by mouth, every six hours, and not more than four doses in a day. Don't stack ibuprofen on top tonight unless she's miserable and won't drink, and if you do, not on an empty stomach. One drug, proper dose, is enough for now.
[SEG0030] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She spat the syringe out last winter, but ja, we'll try it. I can hold her.

[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. On the clear chest and the red throat, my working impression is a viral upper respiratory infection. I still can't fully shut the door on an early bacterial infection if the fever climbs or she starts labouring to breathe, but I'm not calling it that today.
[SEG0032] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So no antibiotics at all? Can she go to crèche tomorrow? And if the fever spikes tonight, do I go straight to casualty or wait?

[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): No antibiotics today. Keep her out of crèche while the fever's there, fluids little and often, and the Panado the way I just said. If she is struggling to breathe, if she goes blue around the lips, or if she stops drinking, that's casualty, don't phone first. Otherwise I want to see her again if she is not better in three days.
[SEG0034] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Three days is ages if it turns out borderline like that x-ray. Shouldn't we just do bloods to be safe? I'm sorry, I know I'm asking too much, I'm just anxious.

[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bloods won't change a single thing I do this afternoon, so I'm not ordering them. That old borderline comment is a story, not a result I'm treating. Any rash on her, or any diarrhoea?
[SEG0036] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No rash. No diarrhoea. She did a wee this morning, the colour looked normal, I think. I didn't keep it or anything.
[SEG0037] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And she's not been pulling at her ears. I checked while we were waiting, before you even ask.

[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, that helps. So, home, the syringe not a spoon from the drawer, and come back if she is not better in three days. If you're worried sooner, phone the rooms, don't sit with it.
[SEG0039] person_4 (PATIENT): Home now?
[SEG0040] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes, my girl, home now. Thank you, Doctor. I'll fetch the syringe at the chemist on the way. Ma, I'm sorry about the squabble.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're both fine. Keep her close tonight.

spec.situation: Parent brings a toddler or school-age child with fever and cough; the two parents (or parent and grandparent) disagree about how long, how high, and what was given (paracetamol vs ibuprofen, doses by 'spoon'). Child says only a few words.
features: test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

bad.reason: Fever is current, but duration is disputed/not confirmed as exactly 3 days.
